patient_information: A 64-year-old Japanese man with a medical history of hypertension and a prior right cerebellar infarction. He also had a history of recent simple partial seizures that were well controlled with an antiepileptic agent.
chief_complaint: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures followed by weakness of the right lower extremity.
history_of_present_illness: The patient was admitted to a hospital after experiencing generalized tonic-clonic seizures which were followed by weakness in his right lower extremity. His pre-existing simple partial seizures had previously been well controlled by medication.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a resident of Japan. The probable infection route was through the consumption of raw chicken meat, which he reported eating approximately once a month before the onset of the generalized seizure.
vitals: On admission, the patient was afebrile.
physical_exam: Upon admission, the patient's Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was 15/15. The neurological examination did not reveal any abnormality.
labs_and_diagnostics: Initial laboratory results showed no abnormalities, including no eosinophilia or leukocytosis. A head CT revealed a small high-density nodule with an enhanced perifocal low-density area in the left occipital lobe. An MRI of the brain showed a ring-enhancing, tunnel-shaped lesion in the left occipital lobe, a finding described as the "tunnel sign". Angiography was normal aside from a right vertebral artery occlusion consistent with his past stroke. Post-operatively, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) on serum and cerebrospinal fluid revealed strong positivity for Spirometra mansoni.
differential_diagnosis: The differential diagnoses for a space-occupying lesion in the brain include brain tumours or metastases, neurocysticercosis, cerebral schistosomiasis, and paragonimiasis. In immunocompromised patients, cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcomas, and tuberculomas would also be considered.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient underwent an open surgery with craniotomy, during which a live, white, tape-like, worm-like structure was identified and completely removed from the targeted lesion in the brain. After the surgical removal of the worm, the patient was well and had no further seizures at his most recent examination.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is cerebral sparganosis caused by a larva of the tapeworm *Spirometra mansoni*. This diagnosis was established by the surgical removal of a live sparganum larva from a ring-enhancing, tunnel-shaped lesion in the left occipital lobe, which was visualized on MRI. The diagnosis was further confirmed by strongly positive ELISA results for *Spirometra mansoni* in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid.
